tldr: The authors introduce MotorSense, a 100-hour dataset pairing wrist-worn electromyography (EMG) sensors with egocentric video. By linking visual frames and muscle activity via contrastive learning, they significantly boost performance in hand action recognition, 3D hand pose estimation, and contact reconstruction.
hero_caption: Overall framework of MotorSense. In (A), egocentric video and bimanual EMG signals are passed through separate encoders and aligned using CLIP-style contrastive learning (sensorimotor alignment) over identical temporal windows. In (B), the resulting vision model transfers to downstream tasks like action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and contact detection. Additionally, discrete tokens (motor codes) extracted from EMG precisely guide a video diffusion model.
overview:
When humans manipulate objects, they rely not only on what they see, but also on internal motor signals like muscle exertion and fine finger sensations. Conventional computer vision models, however, learn hand actions solely from camera pixels, leaving them vulnerable to severe occlusion and completely blind to contact forces.

To bridge this gap, the authors built MotorSense, a large-scale 100-hour dataset that synchronizes bimanual surface electromyography (EMG) and IMU wristbands with head-mounted egocentric video, centered around everyday kitchen tasks. Because it uses non-invasive wristbands instead of bulky data gloves, hands remain completely free to move naturally while capturing dense, occlusion-free muscle activity.

Using this dataset, the authors perform sensorimotor alignment by aligning video and EMG encoders via CLIP-style contrastive learning. EMG acts as privileged information during pre-training only; at inference time, the resulting vision backbone runs on video alone. Furthermore, they extract discrete "motor codes" from EMG using a VQ-VAE, using them as conditioning signals for an image-to-video diffusion model.

Experimental results show that this pre-trained vision model consistently outperforms conventional video-only self-supervised baselines across action recognition, 3D hand shape reconstruction, and hand contact estimation. In generative tasks, motor codes also enable the synthesis of subtle force adjustments and manipulation details that cannot be captured by text prompts or hand trajectories alone.
contributions: Built and released MotorSense, the world's first 100-hour synchronized dataset combining egocentric video, bimanual surface EMG, and IMU during natural unscripted manipulation.
Established a self-supervised pre-training method via sensorimotor alignment between video and EMG signals, yielding a high-performing visual backbone that requires no EMG at inference time.

Demonstrated that the pre-trained vision model outperforms existing self-supervised video methods across action recognition, 3D hand pose estimation, contact reconstruction, and eight video benchmarks.
Demonstrated that unsupervised discrete motor codes extracted from EMG can condition image-to-video diffusion models to guide fine-grained contact and force nuances.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need Muscle Signals to Understand Hands?
sections.summary: AI trained on video lacks the embodied motor signals essential to human motor control. This paper introduces MotorSense, pairing wrist surface EMG with egocentric video to provide an occlusion-free foundation for hand-environment interactions.
sections.details:
Our dexterity comes not just from visual feedback, but from internal motor sensations of how muscles contract. Modern computer vision, however, tries to infer hand actions purely from shifts in high-dimensional pixel arrays. As a result, it struggles to capture the exact contact forces or fine joint configurations when fingers are occluded behind manipulated objects.

Manual annotations like bounding boxes and action labels are expensive, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. Meanwhile, sensory gloves restrict natural movement by placing physical hardware directly over the palm and fingers.

To overcome these hurdles, the authors turn to surface electromyography (EMG) on the forearm. Surface EMG directly measures electrical muscle activity through the skin, capturing finger flexion, wrist rotation, and contact force as dense signals unaffected by visual occlusion. MotorSense uses lightweight wristbands paired with egocentric smart glasses to capture roughly 100 hours of unscripted daily activities like cooking.

The core technique is sensorimotor alignment: mapping video and EMG into a shared embedding space using CLIP-style contrastive learning. EMG is used as a privileged training signal, and at inference time the vision encoder operates entirely on RGB video alone, allowing seamless transfer to standard computer vision pipelines.

captions.F1: EMG signal variations across hand poses and action phases. Top: distinct, repeatable waveform patterns appear across electrodes for "fist", "point", and "flat" poses. Bottom: the progression of contact—pregrasp, grasp, lift, and hold—is clearly reflected in the evolution of EMG signal amplitudes.

sections.heading: From Gesture Control to Teachers for Visual Representations
sections.summary: Past uses of EMG focused on isolated gesture recognition or VR interfaces, with minimal integration into video representation learning. MotorSense breaks new ground through large-scale unscripted data collection, self-supervised pre-training, and generative video control.
sections.details:
### Evolution of EMG and Gesture Recognition
Because surface EMG worn on the forearm non-invasively tracks finger movements and grip forces, it has long been studied for prosthetic limb control and gesture interfaces in VR/AR. Paired video-EMG datasets like ActionSense do exist, but they remain small, confined to scripted lab settings, and have never been used to drive self-supervised learning of general video backbones.

### Multimodal Signals for Action Understanding
Past efforts to enrich video understanding explored text, audio, body-worn IMUs, 3D skeletal poses, and contact force sensors. However, text captions describe high-level intents like "cut" or "stir" without capturing force. Visual keypoints vanish under occlusion and lack dynamics. EMG directly provides the missing puzzle pieces: continuous, occlusion-free finger articulation and interaction force.

### Overcoming Limits of Existing Hand Datasets
Large-scale egocentric datasets like EPIC-Kitchens and Ego4D feature rich interactions, but manual labels remain coarse and costly. Multi-camera motion capture stages offer high precision, but cannot capture natural, unscripted everyday life. By adopting consumer-ready lightweight EMG bands, MotorSense achieves scalable multimodal collection in natural daily environments.

sections.heading: Contrastive Sensorimotor Alignment and Discrete Motor Codes
sections.summary: The authors present a data collection setup with wrist-worn bands and an InfoNCE contrastive pipeline linking video and EMG into a shared latent space. They also quantize EMG into discrete motor codes using a VQ-VAE to condition video diffusion models for fine-grained manipulation.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Data Collection Setup
Data collection relies on MindRove armbands worn on both wrists. Each band features 8 circular dry stainless-steel electrodes (500 Hz sampling, 24-bit resolution) and a 6-axis IMU (50 Hz). Encircling the flexor and extensor muscle groups captures finger bends, wrist rotations, and muscular exertion comprehensively. Visual inputs come from Meta Project Aria smart glasses and head-mounted smartphones, synchronized to millisecond precision.

### 3.2 Sensorimotor Alignment via Contrastive Learning
Over short $1.5$-second windows, video clips and bimanual EMG+IMU sequences are fed into respective encoders: a Hiera-Base for video, and a 1D CNN combined with a bidirectional LSTM for EMG. Features are projected into a shared 1024-dimensional space, L2-normalized, and optimized using a symmetric InfoNCE loss with cosine similarity. A key design rule is forming training batches strictly from within the *same session* (same participant and environment). This prevents shortcut learning, where the model pairs clips by matching individual anatomical signatures or room backgrounds rather than underlying actions. After pre-training, the EMG encoder is discarded, leaving an enhanced vision backbone for downstream tasks.

### 3.3 Video Diffusion Conditioned on Motor Codes
For generation, unlabelled EMG+IMU signals are fed to a VQ-VAE to extract discrete "motor codes" at 64 tokens per second in an unsupervised manner. An image-to-video diffusion model then takes a single initial RGB frame and the motor code sequence to synthesize subsequent video. Instead of fine-tuning the full diffusion backbone, a HyperNetwork inspired by Video2LoRA dynamically predicts LoRA weights from the motor codes, keeping control lightweight and effective.

sections.heading: Outperforming Visual Baselines in Recognition, 3D Mesh, and Video Synthesis
sections.summary: When evaluated on downstream action recognition, 3D hand pose estimation, and contact reconstruction, the pre-trained vision model beat all purely visual SSL baselines. EMG-conditioned diffusion models also reproduced realistic hand contacts and tool interactions far better than baseline approaches.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Action Recognition and 3D Geometric Tasks
Under frozen linear probing on action recognition benchmarks (EPIC-Kitchens-100, Something-Something v2, Ego-Exo4D), MotorSense significantly outperformed K400 pre-trained weights and video-only SSL baselines trained on the same data (such as $\rho$SimCLR and $\rho$MoCo). On EPIC-Kitchens-100 with a frozen backbone, verb accuracy jumped by $+15.9$ points.
On 3D hand pose estimation using ARCTIC and H2O, hand joint error (MPJPE) dropped by $4.6$ mm on H2O compared to ImageNet initialization. In 3D contact reconstruction, predicting which hand mesh vertices touch objects improved Intersection-over-Union (IoU) by $+4.6$ points over top visual SSL baselines like DenseCL, proving that force-sensitive EMG signals provide valuable inductive bias for geometric understanding.

### 4.2 Latent Space Analysis
t-SNE visualizations of the shared embedding space show that while a modality gap between video and EMG remains, identical actions (e.g., mixing salad or scraping a bowl) cluster tightly by category. Querying the EMG space using a video clip via cosine similarity reliably retrieves matching actions executed by different individuals in completely separate kitchens.

### 4.3 Video Generation with Motor Codes
In image-to-video experiments evaluated on FVD and hand-region LPIPS/PSNR, conditioning on text prompts or video history often hallucinated incorrect actions—such as turning a tofu-stirring motion into ladling, or spreading with a spoon into rotating bread. In contrast, motor code conditioning reliably generated fine-grained hand movements that matched the intended action with high fidelity.

captions.F4: Analysis of the latent space learned through self-supervised alignment. (a) A t-SNE plot shows a modality gap between video and EMG clusters, but (b) cross-modal nearest-neighbor retrieval from a video query (left) to the EMG space (right) correctly identifies the same hand action across different people and backgrounds. (c) Within the EMG space, matching verb categories cluster cleanly without any supervised labels.

Left to right: RGB input, visual baseline without EMG, MotorSense pre-trained (with EMG), and ground truth (GT). The EMG-pre-trained model reconstructs finger placements inside scissors and grip contours around bottles with fidelity very close to ground truth.

sections.heading: The Real Win Comes from Signal Quality, Not Just More Video Data
sections.summary: Controlled comparisons confirm that performance gains stem from the physical force and occlusion-free nature of EMG, rather than simply having extra in-domain kitchen footage. The findings also point toward broader applications in VR/AR, teleoperation, and physical rehabilitation.
sections.details:
The key takeaway of this work is that vision backbones can autonomously learn the mechanical structure of actions by aligning with EMG signals during pre-training.

A natural question arises: did performance improve simply because the model had 100 extra hours of kitchen video? To test this, the authors trained vision-only self-supervised baselines (such as $\rho$SimCLR and DenseCL) on the exact same MotorSense video pool. These video-only baselines barely improved over K400 weights and sometimes degraded performance. In contrast, models aligned with EMG achieved substantial gains across all benchmarks, proving that the advantage comes directly from the privileged motor information in EMG signals.

These findings hold broad potential: developing intuitive interfaces for wrist-worn VR/AR devices, helping collaborative robots interpret human hand actions, digitizing surgical procedures, and assisting in physical rehabilitation.

sections.heading: Appendix: Data Collection Behind the Scenes and In-Depth Ablations
sections.summary: The authors detail fitting protocols and filtering pipelines designed to prevent motion artifacts, along with ablations on electrode count and batch construction that highlight the importance of intra-session sampling and preserving temporal tokens.
sections.details:
### Data Collection Protocols and Pre-processing
Capturing clean biosignals requires strict hygiene and fitting routines. Sessions lasted around one hour, preceded by electrode checks and clench tests to verify signal spikes. Because narrow wrists can cause dry electrodes to lift and produce motion artifacts, snug placement was carefully monitored. Raw signals were filtered with a 10 Hz 4th-order zero-phase Butterworth high-pass filter to remove DC drift and body motion artifacts, followed by per-session z-score normalization.

### Insights from Ablation Studies
Testing architectural and pre-training choices yielded several practical takeaways:
- **Modality**: EMG alone provides strong representations, but adding IMU signals to track wrist translation and rotation yields the best overall scores.
- **Electrode Count**: Downsampling from 8 channels to 4 or 2 sharply degraded action recognition accuracy, showing that a full 8-electrode ring is vital for capturing coordinated muscle activations.
- **Batch Construction**: Sampling negatives across random sessions caused the model to take shortcuts based on skin tone or kitchen background, significantly lowering action recognition performance.
- **Temporal Pooling**: Retaining the 8-frame temporal tokens rather than average-pooling over time during contrastive alignment proved critical for downstream task accuracy.

captions.F7: Video generation comparison when frying tofu in a pan. Conditioning only on past video frames (top) misinterprets the motion as ladling, scooping the tofu up. Motor code conditioning (middle) accurately produces the stirring and frying motion seen in ground truth (bottom).

takeaways: For hand action understanding, wrist surface EMG serves as an effective privileged training signal that bypasses visual occlusions.
Aligning video with EMG during self-supervised pre-training upgrades vision models at zero extra inference cost, since downstream tasks only require camera input.
When contrastively learning biosignals, sampling batches strictly within the same session prevents shortcut learning based on user anatomy or room background.
Quantized motor codes extracted via VQ-VAE provide an effective control signal for video diffusion models to synthesize subtle contact forces and fine finger dexterity.
limitations: The dataset uses consumer-grade 8-channel wristbands, which offer lower muscle separation resolution than clinical high-density EMG arrays (16 to 128+ channels).
Physical wristband sizing can cause electrode lift and noise on smaller wrists, introducing a demographic bias in participant wrist size and gender.
Actions are heavily centered on kitchen environments, leading to noticeable performance drops when transferring to out-of-domain tasks like tool assembly or cleaning.
